title: Public access, not excess, is media problem
author: Richard Harwood
thematic_categories: Press & Media Criticism, Journalism Theory & Practice, Audience & Public Engagement
summary: Richard Harwood's column about the media's problems with public access and engagement. The article extensively references Jay Rosen's work, describing him as a 'New York University journalism professor' who writes about 'citizenship' and the connections between the decline of citizenship and the decline of journalism. Harwood discusses Rosen's observations about the 'culture of entertainment' that competes with newspapers.
excerpt: There are close relationships among the decline of citizenship in this country, the decline of what we used to think of 'news' and the decline of journalism's importance in the life of the nation. Rosen notes correctly that, 'To pick up a newspaper and scan the front page is to feel yourself a member of a world in which politics and public affairs matter.'
tags: newspaper clipping, public journalism, citizenship, media criticism, press decline, 1990s
notes: Source PDF: Daily_Press_1994_06_05_Page_59.pdf. Page 59. Column by Richard Harwood, former ombudsman of The Washington Post. Contains extensive discussion of Rosen's ideas about citizenship, public life, and the press. Also references 'young people, New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen among them.'

title: Journalists say U.S. military's restrictions impeded coverage of Persian Gulf War
author: Associated Press
summary: An Associated Press article reporting on a conference where journalists and experts discussed how the U.S. military's press restrictions impeded coverage of the Persian Gulf War. The article references the conference at which university journalism professors and press critics, including those associated with Jay Rosen's circle, debated the role of the press during wartime.
excerpt: The conference came a day after Secretary of Defense Dick Cheney appeared at a meeting with news executives... journalists said the press, which had been largely excluded, should be 'abandoned' in favor of independent reporting.
tags: newspaper clipping, Gulf War, press freedom, military restrictions, media criticism, 1990s
notes: Source PDF: Daily_Sentinel_1991_09_14_10.pdf. Page 10. AP wire story about journalists' complaints regarding military press restrictions during the Gulf War. The article discusses press freedom themes central to Rosen's work on journalism and democracy.

title: Journalists should champion free speech, not fee speech
author: Lee Kenn More
thematic_categories: Press & Media Criticism, Journalism Theory & Practice
summary: A media column criticizing TV journalists like David Brinkley for accepting paid speaking fees, arguing this undermines public trust in journalism. The article references New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen's prediction that journalists accepting paid speaking fees will erode public confidence, and discusses an article in The New Yorker that named and criticized many prominent journalists for this practice.
excerpt: ...warned of the erosion of public trust in journalism, and concluded with a prediction from New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen. 'You're going to start having character stories about journalists.'
pull_quote: You're going to start having character stories about journalists.

title: Some feel media needs to give Kennedys time, space
author: Michael Vallely
thematic_categories: Press & Media Criticism, Audience & Public Engagement
summary: An article examining media coverage of the JFK Jr. plane crash and death, discussing whether reporters should give the Kennedy family more privacy during their time of grief. Experts including Jay Rosen from the New York University Graduate School of Journalism are quoted about the media's performance and the balance between public interest and family privacy.
excerpt: 'It's been a fine performance,' said Rosen, a media critic. 'It's what we've come to expect in a situation like this.' ...Rosen said even the famous Kennedy desire for privacy and a break from reporters during a time of personal grief... 'What are they ostensibly accomplishing besides adding to the national trauma and the personal tragedy?' Rosen asked.
pull_quote: It's been a fine performance. It's what we've come to expect in a situation like this.
tags: newspaper clipping, JFK Jr., Kennedy family, media coverage, privacy, press ethics, 1990s
notes: Source PDF: Poughkeepsie_Journal_1999_07_22_Page_2A.pdf. Page 2A. Rosen is identified as being from the New York University Graduate School of Journalism and is quoted multiple times about media coverage of the JFK Jr. death. He also commented on the media's presence growing worse: 'It's going to get worse,' Rosen predicted.

author: Elaine Woo

Jay Rosen is mentioned as a professor of media ecology who was a former student and colleague of Postman at NYU.
